name: Blissful ignorance effect
statement: After committing to a choice, people are said to expect better outcomes from vague information than from precise information, a gap that is smaller before they commit.
meaning: The claim is an interaction, not a preference for knowing less. Two things vary: whether the information given is precise or vague, and whether it arrives before an action or after one. Mishra, Shiv and Nayakankuppam say that vague information produces more optimistic outcome expectancies after an action than before it, and that precise information narrows the difference. Their abstract names two goals behind this, the goal of arriving at a desired conclusion and the goal of being accurate. Before acting, a person wants to be right, so precision helps. After acting, the person wants the choice to have been good, and vague wording is loose enough to be read that way. Nothing in the claim says a buyer who is told less will enjoy the product more. It says that the same loose wording buys more optimism once the money has been spent.

origin.who: Himanshu Mishra, Baba Shiv and Dhananjay Nayakankuppam
origin.note: The paper names the effect. Its abstract reports three experiments and states that the pattern arises from the interplay of a directional goal, arriving at a desired conclusion, and an accuracy goal.

evidence: What the original paper did could not be read at first hand for this entry. Oxford Academic answered every request on 21 September 2026 with a Cloudflare bot challenge, not a paywall page, so even the publisher's abstract could not be seen this time. Unpaywall, queried the same day, returns oa_status closed with no repository copy, and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar record the article as closed too. No participant counts, condition means, test statistics or effect sizes are quoted here. The abstract was read at IDEAS/RePEc, which carries it in full. It says this: across three experiments, individuals given vague information are more optimistic of outcomes post-action compared to pre-action, and this difference is attenuated with precise information. The abstract does not name the products or the measures. A press release issued by University of Chicago Press Journals on 15 September 2008 says the three studies had participants deciding about chocolates, hand lotions and animated movies. It quotes the authors saying that people tend to expect more favourable outcomes with vague information after taking an action than before taking it. It gives incomplete nutritional information and sketchy reviews as examples of the vague material. Those design details are at one remove from the paper, and the release sets up no contrast with precise information given before the decision. Figures quoted in later popular summaries, including specific probabilities and percentage gaps, were not found in any document reached for this entry.

replication.headline: No repeat of the three experiments was found, and the paper has been cited about thirty times in eighteen years.
replication.detail: Semantic Scholar lists 30 works citing the 2008 paper and OpenAlex counts 31, both checked on 21 September 2026. All 30 were read by title, year and venue. They are applications and reviews in marketing, auditing, sustainability and finance. Two come closest to the original design. One is a 2023 paper in Psychology and Marketing on when to present an extended warranty, before or after the purchase. The other is a 2022 paper in Sustainability on precise against ambiguous information about green products. Neither could be opened here, Wiley answering with a Cloudflare challenge and MDPI with an Akamai refusal, so neither is counted as a repeat or ruled out as one. The FORRT Replication Database was downloaded again on 21 September 2026. Its FReD table holds 2,164 original-replication pairs and its FLoRA companion 2,940 entries. Neither holds a row for this effect, for the 2008 paper's identifier or for the 2011 follow-up. A Europe PMC search for 'blissful ignorance' returned 202 records, all of them clinical or editorial uses of the phrase. A Crossref search on the title terms with replication returned nothing that repeats the design. OpenAlex was rate-limited before a full citation sweep could be run there, as it was last time. CORE answered with server errors all day. BASE served an Anubis proof-of-work challenge which was solved, though the token did not hold, because this session's egress address changed between requests. PsycINFO and the Journal of Consumer Research's own citing-article list were not searched.

limits: The evidence for this effect is one paper that this entry could not open. Sample sizes are the obvious gap. Consumer laboratory experiments of that period often ran a few dozen students per cell, and whether these did cannot be settled from the abstract or the press release. No effect size for the interaction is available from any source reached here. The mechanism has been tested elsewhere with mixed results. Mishra, Mishra and Shiv later argued in Psychological Science that vague information boosts performance, reporting two laboratory studies and one quasi-field study on mental acuity, physical strength and weight loss. That abstract gives no participant counts, and the article itself was not obtained. Green and van Deemter, who did read it, report that its weight-loss result was conditional. Participants whose scores fell outside the ideal range lost more weight under vague feedback, while those inside the range showed no such difference. Green and van Deemter also object that a range of values is not vague in the standard sense, since an exact range admits no borderline cases. Their own three experiments put vague expressions inside referring noun phrases and timed how quickly hearers picked out the referent. Vagueness had no significant main effect on response time. It helped a little where the referent could be found by comparison and hurt a little where it had to be matched. They conclude that the gains credited to vagueness come from factors that travel with it, such as the avoidance of numbers. Their materials are linguistic rather than commercial, and they do not cite the 2008 paper anywhere. Neither paper repeats the pre-action against post-action comparison that defines the blissful ignorance effect.
misreadings: The popular form of this claim is not the published one. Wikipedia's article opens by saying that people with good information about a product are not expected to be as happy with it as people with less information, and cites Schiffman's textbook Consumer Behavior, page 95, for that sentence and Solomon's textbook of the same name, page 318, for a two-group experiment. It cites no journal article on the effect, and its only tie to the 2008 research is a ScienceDaily report of the same press release. Two changes have crept in along the way. Happiness with a product has replaced expectancy about an outcome, and the before-and-after contrast, which is the whole finding, has dropped out, leaving a bare claim that ignorance is pleasant. Three neighbouring ideas are not this one. The ostrich effect is about declining to look at information a person could have for nothing, and is entry 118 here. Wilful ignorance is a choice to stay uninformed, usually to avoid a moral or financial obligation, and the blissful ignorance effect involves no such choice: the information is handed to everybody, and only its precision differs. Choice-supportive bias, entry 169, concerns memory of the option's features after the fact, not predictions about how it will turn out. The forecast being distorted here is about a future outcome, which places the claim beside affective forecasting, entry 161, rather than inside it, since affective forecasting concerns how strongly the event will be felt rather than whether it will go well.
